laws.title: Distracted Driving — Handheld Device Ban
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act (Nunavut) — Fines up to $400
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut prohibits use of handheld electronic devices while driving. Hands-free operation is required. Distracted driving penalties include demerit points and licence suspension for repeat offenders.
laws.penalty: $400 fine + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Hands-free (Bluetooth/speakerphone with phone mounted)
Emergency calls to 911
Police, fire, paramedics on duty

quiz.q: What is the maximum fine for a first distracted driving offence in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut's distracted driving penalty is $400 + 3 demerit points.

laws.title: Hunting & Fishing Licence Requirements
laws.subtitle: Wildlife Act (Nunavut) — Annual licence required
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut requires residents and non-residents to obtain valid provincial licences before hunting or fishing. Residents pay lower fees than non-residents. Licences are required for most species.
laws.penalty: Hunting/fishing without a licence: fines from $200 up to $25,000 + possible equipment seizure.
exceptions: Licence-exempt fishing events designated by province
Indigenous peoples exercising treaty rights
Children under minimum age on licensed adult's supervision

quiz.q: Which group is generally exempt from Nunavut's hunting and fishing licence requirements?
quiz.explanation: Indigenous peoples exercising treaty and Aboriginal rights are generally exempt from provincial licensing requirements.

laws.title: Impaired Driving — Criminal Code Offence
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 320.14 — BAC ≥ 0.08 is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Impaired driving is a federal Criminal Code offence across all of Canada. A blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.08% or higher is per se illegal. Nunavut also enforces a warn range (0.05–0.079) under provincial highway traffic law triggering immediate administrative sanctions. The warn range (0.05–0.079) triggers administrative penalties (licence suspension, remedial program) under provincial law.
laws.penalty: Criminal conviction: minimum $1,000 fine (1st offence), 30 days jail (2nd), 120 days jail (3rd+). Licence suspension (1 year 1st offence). Ignition interlock required.
exceptions: BAC below 0.05%
Zero-tolerance applies to novice/young drivers (under 22 in most provinces) and commercial drivers

quiz.q: What BAC level triggers a Criminal Code impaired driving charge in Canada?
quiz.explanation: Canada's Criminal Code sets 0.08% BAC as the per se criminal threshold for impaired driving nationwide.

laws.title: Open Alcohol in Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Liquor Act (Nunavut) — No open liquor in passenger area
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut prohibits open containers of alcohol in the passenger compartment of a vehicle. Sealed containers must be stored in the trunk or cargo area. Open liquor in a vehicle is prohibited regardless of whether vehicle is moving.
laws.penalty: Fine up to $200 (first offence); increase for repeat violations.
exceptions: Sealed, unopened containers stored in trunk
Passengers in commercial vehicles (buses, taxis, limousines)
Camping or recreational vehicles where the driver is not operating

quiz.q: Where must sealed alcohol containers be stored in a vehicle in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: Open alcohol in the passenger area is illegal; sealed containers must go in the trunk or cargo area.

laws.title: Recreational Cannabis — Federal Legalization
laws.subtitle: Cannabis Act, SC 2018, c. 16 — Legal for adults 19+ (19+ in Nunavut)
laws.fullDescription: Canada legalized recreational cannabis nationwide under the Cannabis Act in October 2018. Adults may legally possess up to 30 grams of dried cannabis (or equivalent) in public. Nunavut minimum cannabis age is 19. Adults may possess up to 30 g. Home cultivation of up to 4 plants permitted. Many communities in Nunavut have opted out of cannabis retail through plebiscite.
laws.penalty: Possession over 30 g: cannabis offence. Distribution to youth: serious Criminal Code offence.
exceptions: Adults 19+ possessing up to 30 g (dried) in public
Home cultivation up to 4 plants per household (federal rule; {s['cannabis_home_grow']})
Medical cannabis patients may exceed limits with valid authorization

quiz.q: What is the legal age for recreational cannabis in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: The federal Cannabis Act sets 18 as a minimum but provinces can raise it. Nunavut sets the minimum at 19.

laws.title: Medical Cannabis Access
laws.subtitle: Cannabis Regulations, SOR/2018-144 — Federal medical program
laws.fullDescription: Medical cannabis is federally regulated in Canada. Patients with a medical document from a health care practitioner may register with a licensed producer to obtain cannabis for medical purposes. There is no provincial-level medical cannabis card — it's a federal program. Patients may possess amounts consistent with their medical document, potentially exceeding the 30-gram recreational limit.
laws.penalty: Possession beyond authorized amount: subject to Cannabis Act penalties.
exceptions: Registered medical patients with valid medical document
Veterans may access medical cannabis through Veterans Affairs Canada

quiz.q: How is medical cannabis access governed in Canada?
options: Each province runs its own program
It is a federal program through licensed producers
quiz.explanation: Medical cannabis in Canada is a federal program — patients register directly with federally licensed producers.

laws.title: Firearms — Possession and Acquisition Licence
laws.subtitle: Firearms Act, SC 1995, c. 39 — PAL required for all firearms
laws.fullDescription: Canada requires a Possession and Acquisition Licence (PAL) to own any firearm. Non-restricted firearms (rifles, shotguns) require a regular PAL; restricted firearms (handguns, semi-auto centrefire rifles) require a restricted PAL and registration. Handguns were subject to a freeze on new civilian sales/transfers since October 2022 (Bill C-21). Long guns require PAL; restricted firearms require restricted PAL and registration.
laws.penalty: Possessing a firearm without a valid PAL: up to 5 years imprisonment (indictable) or up to 2 years less a day (summary).
exceptions: Licensed PAL holders
Exemptions for Indigenous peoples hunting for food under treaty rights
Antique firearms (pre-1898) in some categories

quiz.q: What document is required to legally possess any firearm in Canada?
quiz.explanation: The Possession and Acquisition Licence (PAL) is required for all firearms in Canada — unlike the US, there is no constitutional right to bear arms.

laws.title: Firearms — Background Checks & Safe Storage
laws.subtitle: Firearms Act s. 5–8 — Mandatory background check for PAL
laws.fullDescription: All PAL applicants undergo a mandatory RCMP background check covering criminal history, mental health, domestic violence, and other public safety factors. Safe storage of all firearms is mandatory nationwide — loaded/accessible storage is illegal. Handguns were subject to a freeze on sale/transfer since 2022.
laws.penalty: Improper storage: up to 2 years imprisonment. Providing false information to obtain PAL: criminal offence.
exceptions: Antique firearms (pre-1898) in certain categories
Certain replica firearms

quiz.q: What agency conducts background checks for Canadian firearm licences?
quiz.explanation: The RCMP administers the PAL background check process through the Canadian Firearms Program.

laws.title: Self-Defence — Criminal Code Standard
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 34 — Proportionate force; no Stand Your Ground
laws.fullDescription: Canadian law (s. 34 Criminal Code) permits self-defence when a person believes on reasonable grounds they face a threat and their defensive act is reasonable in the circumstances. Unlike many US states, Canada has no 'Stand Your Ground' law — courts consider whether retreat was possible as one factor in assessing reasonableness. Courts consider all circumstances, including whether there was an opportunity to retreat, under the proportionality analysis.
laws.penalty: Excessive force used in claimed self-defence can result in assault or homicide charges.
exceptions: Defending oneself from imminent unlawful force
Defending others from imminent unlawful force
Defending property in some circumstances (s. 35)

quiz.q: Does Canada have a 'Stand Your Ground' law like some US states?
options: Yes, but only in rural areas
No — proportionality and context (including retreat) govern self-defence
quiz.explanation: Canada has no Stand Your Ground doctrine. Self-defence must be proportionate; the possibility of retreat is one factor courts consider.

laws.title: Minimum Wage — Nunavut
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act (Nunavut) — $19.00/hour (2024)
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut's minimum wage is $19.00 per hour as of 2024. Nunavut's minimum wage is $19.00/hour — the highest in Canada, reflecting extreme northern cost of living. The federal minimum wage (for federally regulated workers) is $17.30/hour (2024), indexed to inflation.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay minimum wage: employer subject to fines and back-pay orders under employment standards.
exceptions: Federally regulated industries follow the federal minimum wage ($17.30/hr)
Some student/young worker rates may vary
Tip credits do not apply in most Canadian provinces

quiz.q: What is Nunavut's provincial minimum wage as of 2024?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut's minimum wage is $19.00/hour as of 2024.

laws.title: Employment Termination — Just Cause or Notice Required
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act (Nunavut) — Employers cannot terminate without cause or notice
laws.fullDescription: Unlike US at-will employment, Nunavut (and all Canadian provinces) requires employers to provide reasonable notice or pay in lieu of notice when terminating without just cause. Nunavut provides notice or pay in lieu based on tenure. 'Just cause' dismissal (no notice, no severance) requires serious misconduct.
laws.penalty: Failure to provide notice/pay: Ministry of Labour order, fines up to $100,000 for corporations.
exceptions: Probationary employees (notice may not apply within probationary period)
Employees with fixed-term contracts
Constructive dismissal cases may entitle employees to treat themselves as terminated

quiz.q: What distinguishes Canadian employment termination law from US 'at-will' employment?
options: Canada requires just cause or reasonable notice/severance for termination
Only unionized employees have termination protections
Termination without cause is a criminal offence
quiz.explanation: Canadian employment law protects workers: termination requires either just cause (serious misconduct) or reasonable notice/pay in lieu — there is no at-will employment.

laws.title: Union Rights & Collective Bargaining
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act (Nunavut) — Right to organize and bargain collectively
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut guarantees workers the right to join unions and bargain collectively. Nunavut workers have collective bargaining rights. Many Inuit workers are represented by territorial unions. The province does not have right-to-work legislation — union security clauses in collective agreements are permitted and commonly used.
laws.penalty: Interference with union rights: unfair labour practice complaints, fines, reinstatement orders.
exceptions: Managerial and confidential employees may be excluded
Agricultural workers in some provinces have limited rights
Federal employees fall under the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act

quiz.q: Does Canada have 'right-to-work' laws like some US states?
options: No — union security clauses are generally enforceable in Canada
Right-to-work applies only to federal employees
quiz.explanation: Canada does not have right-to-work laws. Union security clauses (requiring dues payment) are generally legal and enforceable across Canadian provinces.

laws.title: Non-Compete Agreements
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act / Common Law — Enforceability varies; restrictive covenants scrutinized
laws.fullDescription: Canadian courts apply strict scrutiny to non-compete agreements. They must be reasonable in geographic scope, duration, and activity restricted. Nunavut: Common law test applies. Non-solicitation clauses are more readily enforced than full non-competes.
laws.penalty: Overly broad non-competes are struck down as unenforceable restraints of trade.
exceptions: Non-solicitation (client/employee poaching) clauses more readily enforced
Reasonable non-competes protecting legitimate business interests
Sale-of-business non-competes treated more leniently

quiz.q: How do Canadian courts generally treat non-compete agreements?
options: They are always enforceable if signed
They are illegal in all provinces
They are scrutinized strictly and must be reasonable in scope/duration
quiz.explanation: Canadian courts treat non-competes as restraints of trade and enforce them only if they are reasonable in scope, duration, and geographic area.

laws.title: Paid Sick Leave — Nunavut
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act — 5 (unpaid) paid sick days
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut provides unpaid sick leave; no territorial paid sick day mandate. Federally regulated workers are entitled to 10 paid sick days under the Canada Labour Code (since 2023).
laws.penalty: Failure to provide: ESA complaint, back pay.
exceptions: Federally regulated workers fall under Canada Labour Code (10 paid days)
New employees may have waiting periods
Employers may provide more generous policies

quiz.q: How many paid sick days are Nunavut employees entitled to under provincial law?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut provides 5 (unpaid) paid sick days provincially. Federally regulated workers get 10 days under the Canada Labour Code.

laws.title: Employment Insurance — Federal Program
laws.subtitle: Employment Insurance Act, SC 1996, c. 23 — Federal EI
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Employment Insurance (EI) program is federally administered. Workers who lose their job through no fault of their own (layoff, shortage of work) may claim EI benefits after accumulating the required insurable hours (420–700 hours depending on regional unemployment rate). Benefits are 55% of average insurable earnings, up to a maximum of $668/week (2024).
laws.penalty: EI fraud: repayment plus 3× penalty amount, possible criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Self-employed workers may opt into EI voluntarily
Parental/maternity benefits also available through EI
Sick benefits (15 weeks) and caregiving benefits available

quiz.q: What percentage of average insurable earnings does Canadian EI typically pay?
quiz.explanation: EI pays 55% of average insurable earnings up to the annual maximum insurable amount.

laws.title: Workers' Compensation — WSCC (Workers' Safety and Compensation Commission — NWT & Nunavut)
laws.subtitle: Workers' Compensation Act (Nunavut) — No-fault workplace injury coverage
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut's workers' compensation system provides no-fault coverage for workplace injuries and occupational diseases. The WSCC (Workers' Safety and Compensation Commission — NWT & Nunavut) administers claims. WSCC provides no-fault workplace injury coverage for Nunavut workers. In exchange for coverage, injured workers generally cannot sue their employer.
laws.penalty: Employer failure to register: fines + retroactive premiums.
exceptions: Independent contractors may not be covered (varies)
Certain industries or farm workers may have separate rules
laws.sourceLabel: WSCC (Workers' Safety and Compensation Commission — NWT & Nunavut)

quiz.q: What is the name of Nunavut's workers' compensation board?
options: WSCC (Workers' Safety and Compensation Commission — NWT & Nunavut)
quiz.explanation: Nunavut's workers' compensation is administered by the WSCC (Workers' Safety and Compensation Commission — NWT & Nunavut).

laws.title: Independent Contractor vs. Employee Classification
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act / CRA — Misclassification risks
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut uses a multi-factor test to distinguish employees from independent contractors. Multi-factor test applies. Workers misclassified as contractors may be entitled to full employment standards protections, back pay, and benefits.
laws.penalty: Employer penalties: back pay, benefits, EI/CPP contributions owed, employment standards fines.
exceptions: Genuine contractors with business-like arrangements
Written contractor agreements (helpful but not determinative)

quiz.q: Who ultimately decides if a worker is an employee or independent contractor in Canada?
options: Courts/tribunals apply a multi-factor test based on the actual relationship
CRA has no jurisdiction over provincial workers
quiz.explanation: Courts and tribunals look at the actual working relationship — not just the written contract — to determine proper classification.

laws.title: Child Labour — Minimum Working Age
laws.subtitle: Labour Standards Act — Minimum age 16
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Minimum working age 16 in Nunavut for most employment. Federally regulated industries follow the Canada Labour Code minimum age of 17 for most work.
laws.penalty: Employer violations: ESA fines.
exceptions: Light work exceptions for younger teenagers in some sectors
Farming/family business may have different rules
Entertainment industry requires permits for minors

quiz.q: What is the general minimum working age for most jobs in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: In Nunavut, the general minimum working age is 16, with restrictions on hours and types of work for minors.

laws.title: Pay Equity — Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value
laws.subtitle: Human Rights Act (Nunavut) — Equal pay through Human Rights Act
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut relies on Human Rights Act for pay equity complaints; no standalone legislation. The federal Pay Equity Act (2021) applies to federally regulated employers with 10+ employees, requiring proactive pay equity plans.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance: orders to pay compensation, fines for employers.
exceptions: Small employers may be phased in
Pay equity distinct from 'equal pay for equal work' — broader concept
Federally regulated employers follow the federal Pay Equity Act

quiz.q: What does 'pay equity' require beyond simply equal pay for identical jobs?
options: Equal pay for work of equal value across gender-dominated job classes
quiz.explanation: Pay equity mandates equal pay for work of 'equal value' — comparing predominantly female job classes with male-dominated ones of similar value, not just identical roles.

laws.title: Human Rights — Anti-Discrimination Protections
laws.subtitle: Human Rights Act (Nunavut) + Canadian Human Rights Act (federal)
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut's Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, and services based on protected grounds including race, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability, religion, and more. Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on protected grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity. Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (Inuit traditional knowledge) informs territorial governance. The Canadian Human Rights Act applies to federally regulated industries.
laws.penalty: Human rights complaints: remedies include reinstatement, compensation, policy changes, and public interest remedies.
exceptions: Bona fide occupational requirements (BFOR) defence
Special programs promoting equality not considered discriminatory
Religious organizations may have limited exemptions in some provinces

quiz.q: Which body handles human rights complaints in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut's Human Rights Commission and Tribunal handle complaints of discrimination in employment, housing, and services.

laws.title: Landlord Entry — Notice Required
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act (Nunavut) — 24 hours notice required
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut requires landlords to give 24 hours written notice before entering a rental unit for non-emergency purposes. Landlord must give 24 hours notice for non-emergency entry. Public housing dominates Nunavut's rental market.
laws.penalty: Illegal entry: tenant complaint to LTB.
exceptions: Emergencies (fire, flood, serious damage)
Tenant consents to immediate entry
Final inspection upon lease end with mutual agreement

quiz.q: How much notice must a landlord give before entering a rental unit in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut requires 24 hours written notice before a landlord may enter a rental unit, except in emergencies.

laws.title: Security Deposit / Rent Deposit
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act — Maximum deposit: 1 month's rent
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut permits security deposits up to 1 month's rent. Most residents are in government housing. Deposits must be held in trust and returned with interest within within 10 days of the tenancy ending.
laws.penalty: Excess deposit: LTB complaint, return + interest.
exceptions: Pet damage deposits may apply separately in some provinces
Last month's rent deposits common in Ontario/BC

quiz.q: What is the maximum security deposit allowed in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: In Nunavut, the maximum security deposit is 1 month's rent.

laws.title: Rent Increases — No rent control (but most housing is public)
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act — No rent control; most Nunavut housing is social/public
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut has no rent control for private rentals. However, the vast majority of Nunavummiut live in Nunavut Housing Corporation (NHC) units where rents are income-based.
laws.penalty: Above-guideline increase without LTB approval: tenant complaint, rollback + fines.
exceptions: NHC (public) housing rents are income-tested
Private rental market is very small

quiz.q: Does Nunavut have rent control or rent increase limits?
options: No limits — landlords may raise rent any amount
quiz.explanation: Nunavut has no private rent control. Most residents live in public housing (NHC) where rents are income-based.

laws.title: Eviction — Notice & Process
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act — Formal process required
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Landlords must apply to the Rental Officer for eviction orders. Self-help eviction (changing locks, removing belongings) is illegal. Landlords must obtain an order from the Rental Officer (Nunavut).
laws.penalty: Self-help eviction: criminal offence; damages to tenant.
exceptions: Tenant can remedy non-payment before eviction in most provinces
Illegal eviction: landlord liable for tenant's damages
Certain humanitarian protections for vulnerable tenants

quiz.q: What is the legal way for a landlord to evict a tenant in Canada?
options: Obtaining a formal eviction order from a tribunal
quiz.explanation: Self-help eviction is illegal in all Canadian provinces. Landlords must obtain a formal eviction order through the provincial tenancy tribunal.

laws.title: Short-Term Rentals (Airbnb/VRBO)
laws.subtitle: Municipal by-laws — Minimal regulation
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Short-term rentals in Nunavut largely unregulated; housing shortage makes STRs a sensitive community issue. Many municipalities layer additional requirements on top of provincial rules.
laws.penalty: Operating without required permit: municipal fines.
exceptions: Commercial hotels/B&Bs under separate licensing
Rural/remote areas may have fewer restrictions
Occasional rental of primary residence generally permitted

quiz.q: Are short-term rentals (like Airbnb) regulated in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: Short-term rentals in Nunavut are regulated with registration or permit requirements. Minimal formal regulation given extreme housing shortage.

laws.title: Property Tax — Municipal Assessment
laws.subtitle: Property Assessment and Taxation Act (Nunavut) — Avg effective rate: 1.5%
laws.fullDescription: Property taxes in Nunavut are set by municipalities based on assessed property value. Property taxes in Nunavut are managed territorially and by hamlets. Rates are among the highest in Canada reflecting extreme infrastructure costs. The province sets assessment methodology while municipalities set tax rates.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay: interest charges, eventual tax sale of property.
exceptions: Agricultural land may have preferential rates
Some seniors/low-income programs for deferrals
New construction may have phase-in periods

quiz.q: Who sets residential property tax rates in Nunavut?
options: Municipal governments based on provincial assessment
quiz.explanation: In Nunavut, municipalities set property tax rates based on assessed values determined by the provincial assessment authority.

laws.title: Land Transfer Tax
laws.subtitle: No land transfer tax — No LTT in Nunavut
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut has no land transfer tax. Land in Nunavut is largely crown/Inuit-owned; private property sales are limited. Land transfer taxes apply when property changes hands.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay: CRA/Ministry of Finance audit, penalties.
exceptions: Nominal registration fees only

quiz.q: Does Nunavut have a provincial land transfer tax?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut has no land transfer tax. Land tenure in Nunavut is complex, with most land under Inuit or Crown ownership.

laws.title: Provincial Income Tax — Nunavut
laws.subtitle: Income Tax Act (Nunavut) — Top rate: 11.5%
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut levies provincial income tax on residents in addition to federal income tax. Nunavut has the lowest top territorial income tax rate in Canada at 11.5%, providing a cost-of-living offset for northern residents. Combined federal-provincial top marginal rates in Nunavut are approximately 44.5%.
laws.penalty: Failure to file/pay: CRA interest + penalties; provincial enforcement.
exceptions: Basic personal amounts reduce taxable income
Various provincial credits and deductions available
Federal RRSP/TFSA rules apply nationwide

quiz.q: What is Nunavut's top provincial income tax rate?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut's top provincial income tax rate is 11.5%, on incomes over $173,205+.

laws.title: Sales Tax — GST only (no territorial sales tax)
laws.subtitle: Federal GST only — Combined rate: 5%
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut has no territorial sales tax — only the federal 5% GST applies. Northern Residents Deductions provide federal tax relief. The federal GST is 5% and applies nationwide. 5% federal GST only
laws.penalty: Businesses must collect and remit applicable taxes; failure results in CRA audits and penalties.
exceptions: Basic groceries, prescription drugs, and medical devices are GST/HST-exempt
Children's clothing, books often exempt from PST in some provinces
Farmers and certain exporters may claim exemptions

quiz.q: What is the total sales tax rate on most goods and services in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: In Nunavut, the total sales tax is 5% (5% GST only).

laws.title: Probate & Estate Administration
laws.subtitle: Probate Rules (Nunavut Court of Justice) — Probate fees + no estate tax
laws.fullDescription: Canada has no federal estate tax or inheritance tax. Nunavut charges probate fees/administration taxes on the value of an estate passing through probate. Nunavut probate handled through the Court of Justice; fees are modest. Surviving spouses/common-law partners receive preferential treatment.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay EAT: interest and penalties.
exceptions: Assets with named beneficiaries (RRSPs, insurance) bypass probate
Joint tenancy property passes by survivorship
Trusts can avoid probate

quiz.q: Does Canada have a federal estate or inheritance tax?
options: No — Canada has no estate or inheritance tax
quiz.explanation: Canada has no federal estate or inheritance tax. Estates face probate fees and the deemed disposition rule at death (capital gains), but no estate tax.

laws.title: Smoke-Free Public Spaces
laws.subtitle: Tobacco and Vapour Products Control Act (Nunavut) — Smoking banned in public enclosed spaces
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut bans smoking in enclosed public spaces, workplaces, and vehicles with minors present. Nunavut bans smoking in enclosed public spaces. Community wellness programs address tobacco use rates, which are among the highest in Canada. E-cigarettes and vaping are generally regulated similarly to smoking.
laws.penalty: Individual: $250 first offence up to $100,000. Proprietor: up to $300,000.
exceptions: Designated outdoor smoking areas may be permitted
Private residences (adults only)
Some Indigenous ceremonial uses

quiz.q: Is smoking banned in indoor workplaces and public spaces in Nunavut?
options: Yes — all enclosed public spaces and workplaces
quiz.explanation: Nunavut bans smoking in all enclosed public spaces and workplaces.

laws.title: Helmet Law — Cyclists & Motorcyclists
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act (Nunavut) — Mandatory helmet requirements
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut requires all cyclists to wear helmets. Motorcycle helmets mandatory. Cycling is limited in northern communities. Motorcycle helmets are required for all riders. Cyclist helmet requirements vary by province.
laws.penalty: No helmet: $60–$500 fine.
exceptions: No exemptions.

quiz.q: Who is required to wear a helmet while cycling in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut requires all cyclists to wear approved helmets.

laws.title: Seatbelt Law — Mandatory Use
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act (Nunavut) — All occupants must wear seatbelts
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut requires all vehicle occupants to wear seatbelts. Primary enforcement — police can stop vehicles solely for seatbelt violations. All occupants required; driver responsible for passengers under 16.
laws.penalty: Driver: $200–$1,000 + 2 demerits. Passenger 16+: $200–$1,000.
exceptions: Medical exemption with doctor's certificate
Children must use approved child safety seats until minimum height/weight/age
Vehicles manufactured before seatbelt requirements may be exempt

quiz.q: Who is responsible for ensuring child passengers are properly buckled in a vehicle?
quiz.explanation: The driver is legally responsible for ensuring all passengers, especially children in safety seats, are properly restrained.

laws.title: Speed Limits — Default Limits
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act — 100 km/h on 400-series highways
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut default speed limits: 100 km/h on territorial highways (where they exist); 50 km/h in communities. Most inter-community travel is by air. Photo radar/automated enforcement used in school/construction zones in many provinces.
laws.penalty: Speeding: fines from $2.50/km over to $9.75/km over 50 km/h above limit (stunt driving).
exceptions: Posted limits supersede defaults
Emergency vehicles
Construction zone speeds mandatory when workers present

quiz.q: What is the default highway speed limit in Nunavut where not otherwise posted?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut's default highway speed limit is 100 km/h.

laws.title: Texting While Driving — Prohibited
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act — Handheld ban covers texting
laws.fullDescription: Texting while driving is prohibited across all Canadian provinces under distracted/handheld device laws. Nunavut: Handheld ban covers texting, browsing, and all handheld device use.
laws.penalty: Same as distracted driving: $615–$3,000 + demerit points.
exceptions: Hands-free voice texting permitted
Emergency 911 use permitted
Parked vehicle (engine off) generally exempt

quiz.q: Is texting while driving prohibited in Canada?
options: Yes — province-wide ban on handheld use including texting
Only when school zones are active
quiz.explanation: Texting while driving is prohibited under provincial distracted driving laws across all Canadian provinces.

laws.title: DUI Sobriety Checkpoints — RIDE Program
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 320.27 + provincial authority — Checkpoints legal
laws.fullDescription: Unlike some US states, random sobriety checkpoints are fully legal across Canada. Nunavut participates in RIDE (Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere) programs. Police may stop any vehicle at a checkpoint and demand a roadside breath sample. The Supreme Court of Canada upheld checkpoints in R v Ladouceur (1990).
laws.penalty: Refusal to provide breath sample: same penalty as impaired driving (Criminal Code s. 320.15).
exceptions: The right to remain silent does not apply to roadside breath demands
Drivers may request a lawyer after a positive roadside test

quiz.q: Are random DUI sobriety checkpoints (RIDE programs) legal in Canada?
options: Yes — upheld by Supreme Court of Canada
quiz.explanation: The Supreme Court upheld random checkpoints in R v Ladouceur (1990). RIDE programs are a well-established tool across Canada.

laws.title: Move Over / Slow Down for Emergency Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act — Mandatory slow-down/lane change
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut requires drivers approaching stationary emergency vehicles (police, fire, ambulance, tow trucks) with flashing lights to slow down and move to an adjacent lane if safe to do so. Must slow to 60 km/h (or posted limit if lower) and move over when safe to do so.
laws.penalty: Fine: $400–$2,000 + 3 demerits.
exceptions: If lane change not safe, slow to well below speed limit
Applies to tow trucks and utility vehicles in many provinces

quiz.q: What must drivers do when approaching a stationary emergency vehicle with lights flashing?
options: Slow down and move to an adjacent lane if safe
Maintain speed — it's the officer's responsibility
quiz.explanation: Move over laws require slowing and moving lanes (if safe) when passing stationary emergency or tow-truck vehicles with lights activated.

laws.title: Handheld Cell Phone Use While Driving
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act — Handheld banned; hands-free allowed
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut bans all handheld use of electronic devices while driving. Drivers caught holding a phone at red lights face the same penalties as moving violations. Demerit points apply in addition to fines.
laws.penalty: Same as distracted driving fines.
exceptions: Hands-free device use permitted
GPS devices (mounted) permitted
Contacting 911 in emergency permitted

quiz.q: Can a driver use a handheld cell phone at a red light in Nunavut?
options: No — handheld ban applies even when stopped at lights
quiz.explanation: Handheld bans apply even when stopped at red lights in all Canadian provinces.

laws.title: Age of Majority — Nunavut
laws.subtitle: Age of Majority Act (Nunavut) — Age of majority: 19
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut's age of majority is 19. At 18, individuals can vote (federal), purchase alcohol, enter binding contracts, and are fully subject to adult criminal law. Most legal rights (voting, contracts, alcohol) attach at the age of majority.
laws.penalty: Minors may be subject to guardianship; contracts with minors generally voidable.
exceptions: Federally, voting age is 18 (Election Act)
Provinces can set their own majority age
Some federal rights (e.g., criminal responsibility) have separate age thresholds

quiz.q: What is the age of majority in Nunavut?
quiz.explanation: The age of majority in Nunavut is 19.

laws.title: Voting Rights — Federal & Provincial
laws.subtitle: Canada Elections Act + provincial election acts — Age 18
laws.fullDescription: Canadian citizens aged 18+ are entitled to vote in federal elections (Canada Elections Act). Nunavut: Nunavut territorial elections: 18+, Canadian citizen, resident. Consensus government — no political parties. Inuktitut is an official language. Indigenous peoples retain full voting rights. Prisoners regained federal voting rights per Sauvé v Canada (2002).
laws.penalty: Voter fraud: fines up to $50,000 and/or 5 years imprisonment (federal).
exceptions: Non-citizens cannot vote in federal elections
Permanent residents can vote in some municipal elections in certain provinces
People under guardianship orders still retain voting rights in most cases

quiz.q: At what age can Canadian citizens vote in federal elections?
quiz.explanation: Canadian citizens must be 18 to vote in federal elections under the Canada Elections Act.

laws.title: Jury Duty — Selection and Obligations
laws.subtitle: Jury Act (Nunavut) — Civic obligation for eligible residents
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Canadian citizens 18+ resident in Nunavut. Federal criminal juries are governed by the Criminal Code; civil juries by provincial rules. Jurors are entitled to compensation for service.
laws.penalty: Failure to attend without excuse: fine or contempt of court.
exceptions: Certain professionals (judges, lawyers, police, doctors in some provinces) exempt
Financial hardship may be grounds for excuse
Non-citizens and non-permanent residents not eligible

quiz.q: Who is eligible for jury duty in Canada?
options: Canadian citizens and permanent residents who are 18+
Any adult who requests to serve
quiz.explanation: Jury eligibility varies by province but generally requires Canadian citizenship and being 18+.

laws.title: Mandatory Reporting — Child Abuse & Neglect
laws.subtitle: Child and Family Services Act (Nunavut) s. 8 — All persons must report
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: All Nunavut residents must report reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect to Child and Family Services. Rates of child welfare involvement are extremely high. Unlike some jurisdictions, Nunavut (like all Canadian provinces) imposes a duty on ALL persons — not just professionals — to report suspected child abuse or neglect to child welfare authorities.
laws.penalty: Failure to report: fine up to $5,000.
exceptions: Good faith reporters are protected from civil liability
Anonymous reports accepted
Reporting does not require certainty — reasonable suspicion is enough

quiz.q: Who is required to report suspected child abuse in Canadian provinces?
quiz.explanation: All Canadian provinces impose a duty on ALL persons (not just professionals) to report suspected child abuse or neglect.

laws.title: Age of Consent — Criminal Code
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 150.1 — Age of consent: 16
laws.fullDescription: Canada's age of consent is 16 (Criminal Code, as amended 2008). There is a 'close-in-age' exception allowing sexual activity between 14–15 year olds and partners less than 5 years older, and between 12–13 year olds and partners less than 2 years older. The age of consent for anal intercourse was harmonized to 16 in 2022. There is no marriage exception — the minimum marriage age is 18 federally.
laws.penalty: Sexual offences involving minors: significant mandatory minimum sentences under the Criminal Code.
exceptions: Close-in-age ('Romeo and Juliet') exceptions (see above)
No exception for positions of trust/authority/dependency — age is raised to 18 for those in authority

quiz.q: What is Canada's federal age of consent for most sexual activity?
quiz.explanation: Canada's Criminal Code sets the age of consent at 16, with close-in-age exceptions for youth 12–15.

laws.title: Emancipation of Minors
laws.subtitle: Child and Family Services Act (Nunavut) — No formal emancipation statute
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: No formal emancipation statute; courts apply best-interests analysis in Nunavut context. Full common-law emancipation (court-ordered) is less formal in Canada than in some US states; courts focus on the minor's best interests.
laws.penalty: Unemancipated minors' contracts are generally voidable.
exceptions: Marriage emancipates for some purposes
Military enlistment (with parental consent)
Living independently with parental consent may achieve de facto emancipation

quiz.q: How is emancipation of minors typically handled in Canadian provinces?
options: Through a formal court petition as in the US
No formal emancipation — courts use best-interests analysis
quiz.explanation: Canadian provinces handle minor emancipation through court proceedings focused on the child's best interests, not a formal US-style emancipation statute.

laws.title: Youth Curfew Laws
laws.subtitle: Municipal By-laws — No provincial curfew
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Ontario has no province-wide youth curfew; some municipalities have their own local curfews for minors. Most Canadian provinces do not have province-wide curfews; some municipalities have overnight curfews for minors.
laws.penalty: Violation of municipal curfew: fine; police may take minor home.
exceptions: Emergency declarations may impose broader curfews
Curfew conditions may be set by courts as bail conditions
Youth working late shifts have implied exception

quiz.q: Are there province-wide youth curfews in Canadian provinces?
options: Generally no — some municipalities have local curfews
quiz.explanation: Most Canadian provinces do not have province-wide youth curfews; some municipalities enact their own local curfews for minors.

laws.title: Corporal Punishment — Criminal Code s. 43
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 43 — Limited parental defence; schools banned
laws.fullDescription: Criminal Code s. 43 provides parents a limited defence for 'reasonable' physical correction of children. The Supreme Court (Canadian Foundation, 2004) upheld s. 43 but narrowed it: only minor corrective force, no objects, not to head/face, only ages 2–12. Corporal punishment in schools has been banned by the SCC ruling and removed from legislation in most provinces. {p}: {s['cp_detail']}
laws.penalty: Excessive force: assault charges. Schools: administrative discipline.
exceptions: Supreme Court limits: ages 2–12 only, no objects, no head/face blows
Must be for corrective purposes, not out of frustration
Many child advocates call for full repeal of s. 43

quiz.q: Can teachers use corporal punishment in Canadian schools?
options: No — corporal punishment in schools has been eliminated
quiz.explanation: The Supreme Court's 2004 ruling effectively banned corporal punishment in schools. Only parents retain a narrowly limited s. 43 defence.

laws.title: Homeschooling — Provincial Regulations
laws.subtitle: Education Act (Nunavut) — Legal with registration
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut permits homeschooling with ministerial approval. Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun instruction may be incorporated. All provinces require children to receive education, whether in school or through approved homeschooling.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with compulsory attendance: fines for parents.
exceptions: Instruction need not follow exact curriculum in all provinces
Parents need not be certified teachers in most provinces
Children with special needs may have additional support options

quiz.q: Is homeschooling legal in Nunavut?
options: Illegal — all children must attend school
quiz.explanation: Homeschooling is legal in Nunavut but requires ministerial approval and submitted educational plan.

laws.title: Vaccination — School Requirements
laws.subtitle: Public Health Act (Nunavut) — Required with exemptions
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut recommends vaccinations. Remote community outreach programs exist given limited health infrastructure. Canada has no federal vaccine mandate; provinces set school immunization requirements.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant students may be suspended from school.
exceptions: Medical exemptions available
Philosophical/religious exemptions vary by province
Parental consent required for minors

quiz.q: Does Nunavut require vaccinations for children to attend school?
quiz.explanation: Nunavut recommends vaccination but does not mandate it for school attendance.

laws.title: Abortion — Decriminalized & Provincially Provided
laws.subtitle: R v Morgentaler [1988] 1 SCR 30 — No criminal prohibition
laws.fullDescription: Abortion has been decriminalized in Canada since the Supreme Court's Morgentaler decision in 1988 — there is no criminal law on abortion. Access is governed by provincial health care systems. Abortion services available in Iqaluit. Residents in remote communities must travel to Iqaluit or southern Canada for access. Abortion is covered under provincial health insurance for medically necessary procedures.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties. Access may be limited by geography/provider availability.
exceptions: Gestational limits may exist for publicly funded procedures in some provinces
Private clinics may offer services beyond hospital gestational limits
Conscientious objection by individual providers is permitted but must not impede access

quiz.q: Is abortion legal in Canada?
options: Decriminalized — no Criminal Code restrictions; access governed provincially
quiz.explanation: Since Morgentaler (1988), there is no criminal restriction on abortion in Canada. Access is a provincial health care matter.

laws.title: Capital Punishment — Abolished Since 1976
laws.subtitle: Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1976 — Death penalty abolished
laws.fullDescription: Canada abolished the death penalty for all civilian crimes in 1976 and for military offences in 1999. The last execution was Ronald Turpin and Arthur Lucas, hanged in 1962. Canada also will not extradite individuals to face the death penalty without assurances it will not be applied. Nunavut, like all Canadian provinces, applies this federal law.
laws.penalty: N/A — capital punishment does not exist in Canada.
exceptions: Canada will not extradite without death penalty assurances
Life imprisonment (25 years before parole eligibility) is the maximum sentence

quiz.q: When was the death penalty abolished in Canada?
quiz.explanation: Canada abolished capital punishment for civilian offences in 1976; the last executions occurred in 1962.

laws.title: Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID)
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 241.2 (Bill C-14/C-7) — Legal with conditions
laws.fullDescription: Canada legalized MAID in 2016 (Bill C-14) following the Carter v Canada SCC ruling. Bill C-7 (2021) expanded eligibility by removing the 'reasonably foreseeable natural death' requirement and creating two tracks. Nunavut follows the federal MAID framework. Access is extremely limited in remote communities; concentrated in Iqaluit. As of 2024, MAID for mental illness as sole underlying condition remains under review.
laws.penalty: Administering MAID outside legal framework: criminal offence.
exceptions: Must be an eligible Canadian resident with a serious and incurable illness/disease/disability
Mental illness as sole condition not yet permitted (as of 2024)
10-day reflection period (Track 1) or 90-day assessment (Track 2)
Conscientious objection by practitioners permitted

quiz.q: What Supreme Court case led to Canada legalizing medical assistance in dying?
quiz.explanation: Carter v Canada (2015) struck down the blanket ban on assisted dying, leading to Bill C-14 legalizing MAID in 2016.

laws.title: Drug Penalties — Controlled Drugs and Substances Act
laws.subtitle: CDSA, SC 1996, c. 19 — Federal drug law
laws.fullDescription: Drug offences in Canada are governed by the federal Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (CDSA). Nunavut applies federal CDSA. Substance abuse is a significant health crisis; many communities have alcohol restrictions. Nunavut has one of Canada's highest rates of drug-related harm. Simple possession of small amounts of most drugs was effectively decriminalized in some provinces through prosecutorial discretion; federal Bill C-5 (2022) eliminated some mandatory minimums.
laws.penalty: Trafficking in Schedule I substance: up to life imprisonment. Simple possession (CDSA): summary — up to $1,000 + 6 months jail; indictable — up to 7 years.
exceptions: Cannabis (legal — Cannabis Act)
Certain medical/pharmaceutical exemptions
Bill C-5 (2022) restored sentencing discretion for some possession offences

quiz.q: What federal law governs most drug offences in Canada (excluding cannabis)?
quiz.explanation: The CDSA governs controlled substance offences in Canada. Cannabis has its own legislation (Cannabis Act) since 2018.

laws.title: Civil Forfeiture — Active program
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code (federal) — Proceeds of crime
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut relies on federal criminal forfeiture; no territorial civil forfeiture legislation. Civil forfeiture allows the government to seize assets alleged to be proceeds of crime — without requiring a criminal conviction.
laws.penalty: N/A — civil proceeding.
exceptions: Innocent owner defence available
Property can be claimed back if owner proves it is unrelated to crime
Burden of proof is civil standard (balance of probabilities)

quiz.q: Does civil forfeiture in Canada require a criminal conviction first?
options: No — civil standard applies; no conviction required
quiz.explanation: Civil forfeiture uses the civil burden of proof — the government need not obtain a criminal conviction before seizing assets.

laws.title: Criminal Record Suspension (Pardon)
laws.subtitle: Criminal Records Act, RSC 1985, c. C-47 — Federal program
laws.fullDescription: Canada uses 'record suspensions' (formerly 'pardons') administered by the Parole Board of Canada. After completing a sentence and a waiting period (5 years for summary offences, 10 years for indictable), eligible individuals may apply to seal their criminal record. Federal record suspensions apply. No separate Nunavut program. Cannabis convictions for simple possession may be expunged (not just suspended) under the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act.
laws.penalty: Record suspension: $657.77 application fee (2024); denial is possible for serious offences.
exceptions: Sexual offences against children: ineligible
Schedule 1 offences: additional scrutiny
Expungement (full erasure) available for historically unjust convictions (e.g., past cannabis possession, consensual same-sex acts)

quiz.q: What is the Canadian term for what Americans call a criminal 'expungement'?
quiz.explanation: Canada uses 'record suspension' (previously called a pardon). Applications go to the Parole Board of Canada after a waiting period.

laws.title: Solitary Confinement — Structured Intervention Units
laws.subtitle: Corrections and Conditional Release Act (as amended 2019) — SIUs
laws.fullDescription: Bill C-83 (2019) eliminated traditional solitary confinement in federal prisons, replacing it with Structured Intervention Units (SIUs). Inmates in SIUs must receive at least 4 hours outside cell daily and 2 hours of meaningful human contact. Nunavut provincial correctional facilities follow: Baffin Correctional Centre subject to territorial corrections legislation and Charter review.
laws.penalty: Violations of SIU standards: complaints to correctional investigator, court challenges.
exceptions: Courts have found extended segregation violates s. 7 and 12 of the Charter
Independent oversight through Institutional Heads and external review

quiz.q: What replaced traditional solitary confinement in Canadian federal prisons?
quiz.explanation: Bill C-83 (2019) replaced administrative segregation with Structured Intervention Units, requiring minimum human contact and out-of-cell time.

laws.title: Private Prisons — Largely Absent in Canada
laws.subtitle: Corrections and Conditional Release Act — Federal prisons public
laws.fullDescription: Unlike the US, Canada has very few private prisons. Federal correctional facilities are operated by Correctional Service Canada (CSC). Nunavut: Nunavut does not operate private prisons. Baffin Correctional Centre is the primary facility. Some immigration detention facilities contract private operators, but these have faced criticism.
laws.penalty: N/A — private prison operation not generally applicable.
exceptions: Some immigration detention involves private contractors
Privately operated halfway houses/community residential facilities exist
Electronic monitoring contracts may be privately operated

quiz.q: Do private prisons operate federal correctional institutions in Canada?
options: Yes — most federal prisons are private
No — federal prisons are operated by Correctional Service Canada
quiz.explanation: Canadian federal prisons are operated by Correctional Service Canada (CSC). Private prisons are not a significant feature of the Canadian corrections system.

laws.title: Police Body-Worn Cameras
laws.subtitle: Varies by police service — Policy varies by police service
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: RCMP (policing Nunavut) has national body camera rollout underway. Unlike some US states, Canada has no province-wide legislation mandating body cameras — policies are set at the police service level.
laws.penalty: Failure to follow body cam policies: disciplinary action; footage admissible in court.
exceptions: RCMP has a national BWC rollout underway
Municipal forces set independent policies
Privacy Act and PIPEDA govern footage retention

quiz.q: Is there a province-wide law mandating body cameras for all police in Canada?
options: No — policies are set at the police service level
Only the RCMP is required to use them
quiz.explanation: Canada has no federal or provincial law mandating body cameras for all police. Each police service sets its own policy, though the RCMP is rolling out cameras nationally.

laws.title: Police Use of Force — Charter & CCRA Standards
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 25 + Charter s. 7, 9, 12 — Proportionate force
laws.fullDescription: Canadian police use-of-force is governed by Criminal Code s. 25 (protection of persons enforcing the law) and the Charter. Force must be reasonable and proportionate. Nunavut: Nunavut policed exclusively by RCMP; oversight through federal channels. Community policing critical in remote areas. The Civilian Review and Complaints Commission oversees RCMP conduct.
laws.penalty: Excessive force: criminal charges (assault, manslaughter, homicide); civil liability; disciplinary action.
exceptions: Officer safety is a factor in proportionality analysis
Use of lethal force requires imminent threat of death/grievous bodily harm
Duty to de-escalate increasingly recognized
laws.sourceLabel: Nunavut Police Act / Criminal Code s. 25

quiz.q: What legal standard governs police use of force in Canada?
options: Officers may use any force needed to effect an arrest
Force must be reasonable and proportionate under Criminal Code s. 25
Only weapons are regulated; physical force is unrestricted
Provincial police set their own standards independently
quiz.explanation: Criminal Code s. 25 and Charter protections require police force to be reasonable and proportionate to the threat faced.

laws.title: Clare's Law — Domestic Violence Disclosure
laws.subtitle: RCMP protocols (Nunavut) — RCMP may disclose risk
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut relies on RCMP protocols for domestic violence risk disclosure; no formal Clare's Law statute. Domestic violence rates are among the highest in Canada. Clare's Law (named after Clare Wood, UK) allows individuals to ask police about a partner's history of domestic violence.
laws.penalty: N/A — disclosure only.
exceptions: Information only disclosed if there is a genuine risk of harm
Disclosure is discretionary in some provincial implementations
Partners may proactively inquire or police may proactively disclose

quiz.q: What does Clare's Law allow individuals to do?
options: Ask police about a partner's history of domestic violence
quiz.explanation: Clare's Law creates a scheme allowing people to ask police if their partner has a history of domestic violence — aiming to prevent further harm.

laws.title: Hate Crimes — Criminal Code Enhancement
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 318–320 + s. 718.2(a)(i) — Enhanced sentencing
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Criminal Code prohibits advocating genocide (s. 318) and public incitement of hatred (s. 319) against identifiable groups. For other offences, evidence of hate motivation can be considered as an aggravating factor at sentencing (s. 718.2). Identifiable groups include race, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, and more. RCMP investigates hate crimes in Nunavut. Racism against Inuit is a documented concern.
laws.penalty: Hate speech (s. 319): up to 2 years. Genocide advocacy (s. 318): up to 5 years. Aggravated sentencing for hate-motivated offences.
exceptions: Truth is a defence to hate speech charges
Private conversation exemption for some communications
Artistic/educational/religious expression may receive Charter protection

quiz.q: What does Criminal Code s. 718.2 do in hate crime cases?
options: Creates a separate hate crime offence
Allows hate motivation to be considered as an aggravating factor at sentencing
quiz.explanation: Section 718.2(a)(i) of the Criminal Code requires courts to treat evidence of hate motivation as an aggravating factor when sentencing.

laws.title: Domestic Violence — Provincial & Criminal Code Protections
laws.subtitle: Family Abuse Intervention Act (Nunavut) + Criminal Code — Assault/threat provisions apply
laws.fullDescription: Domestic violence is addressed through both provincial civil protection orders and federal Criminal Code offences. Nunavut: Nunavut's Family Abuse Intervention Act provides emergency protection orders. Domestic violence rates are extremely high — among the highest in Canada. Emergency Protection Orders (EPOs) can be obtained 24/7 in most provinces without a lawyer.
laws.penalty: Assault: up to 5 years (indictable). EPO violation: up to 2 years.
exceptions: Victims may obtain emergency protection orders quickly
Crown typically prosecutes DV cases even if victim withdraws complaint
Safe houses and transition services available province-wide
laws.sourceLabel: Nunavut Domestic Violence Act / Criminal Code

quiz.q: Can domestic violence charges proceed if a victim decides not to cooperate with prosecution?
options: No — victim can always withdraw charges
Yes — the Crown may proceed independently in the public interest
quiz.explanation: Crown prosecutors in Canada can and often do proceed with domestic violence charges independently of the victim's wishes, in the public interest.

laws.title: Criminal Harassment (Stalking)
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code s. 264 — Criminal harassment
laws.fullDescription: Criminal Code s. 264 prohibits criminal harassment (stalking): repeatedly following, communicating with, watching, or threatening a person causing them to reasonably fear for their safety. Nunavut courts issue peace bonds for criminal harassment. Remote community context affects access to legal remedies. Maximum sentence is 10 years (indictable) or 18 months (summary).
laws.penalty: Summary: up to 18 months. Indictable: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Reporting to police required; peace bonds (recognizance) available
Restraining orders available through provincial family/civil courts
Digital/online stalking (cyberstalking) covered

quiz.q: What is the maximum penalty for criminal harassment (stalking) in Canada?
quiz.explanation: Criminal harassment under Criminal Code s. 264 carries a maximum of 10 years when prosecuted by indictment.

laws.title: Privacy Law — PIPEDA (federal)
laws.subtitle: PIPEDA — No substantially similar law — PIPEDA applies
laws.fullDescription: Federal PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) governs private-sector data collection nationally. Nunavut: Nunavut has no substantially similar private-sector privacy law; PIPEDA applies. Individuals have rights to access and correct personal information held by organizations.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance: OPC investigation, orders to comply, fines (modernized under Bill C-27 if passed).
exceptions: PIPEDA applies as no substantially similar provincial law
Public sector (government) covered by separate Access to Information / Privacy Acts
Health information may be covered by separate provincial health privacy laws

quiz.q: Does Nunavut have its own private-sector privacy law that meets the federal PIPEDA standard?
options: Yes — Nunavut has its own law
quiz.explanation: Nunavut has no substantially similar private-sector privacy law; PIPEDA applies.

laws.title: Social Media Age Verification
laws.subtitle: No specific law — Emerging legislation
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: No Nunavut-specific social media age verification law. Age verification for social media is an emerging area; as of 2024 there is no comprehensive Canadian federal or provincial law, though Bill S-210 (federal) proposed age verification for sexually explicit content.
laws.penalty: Varies — emerging area.
exceptions: Federal Bill S-210 proposed age verification for explicit content
Platforms may self-regulate under terms of service
Privacy considerations complicate mandatory age verification

quiz.q: As of 2024, does Canada have a comprehensive national law requiring age verification for social media?
options: Yes — all provinces have such laws
No — no comprehensive national law exists yet
quiz.explanation: As of 2024, Canada lacks a comprehensive national age verification law for social media. Various proposals (e.g., Bill S-210 for explicit content) are under discussion.

laws.title: Environmental Protection — Federal & Provincial
laws.subtitle: CEPA 1999 + Environmental Protection Act (Nunavut) — Shared jurisdiction
laws.fullDescription: Environmental regulation in Canada is shared between federal (CEPA 1999 — Canadian Environmental Protection Act) and provincial governments. Nunavut: Nunavut's environmental governance addresses unique Arctic challenges including climate change impacts (permafrost thaw, sea ice loss), mining, and Inuit land stewardship. Federal law governs interprovincial/international pollution; provinces manage local environment.
laws.penalty: CEPA violations: up to $1M/day (corporations) or $250K (individuals). Provincial penalties vary.
exceptions: Federal environmental assessment applies to designated projects
Provinces may set stricter standards than federal minimums
Indigenous consultation required for major projects under UNDRIP/Haida Nation

quiz.q: How is environmental jurisdiction divided in Canada?
options: Shared — federal handles inter-jurisdictional/toxic substances; provinces handle local environment
quiz.explanation: Environmental regulation in Canada is shared: the federal CEPA handles toxic substances and interprovincial issues; provinces regulate local environmental matters.

laws.title: Renewable Energy — Nunavut's Grid
laws.subtitle: Qulliq Energy Corporation Act — Almost entirely diesel — transitioning
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut generates electricity almost exclusively from diesel generators in isolated community microgrids. Solar and wind projects are being piloted in some communities. Extremely high costs. Federal Clean Electricity Regulations (proposed) aim for a net-zero grid by 2035. Provincial grids vary widely in carbon intensity.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with renewable portfolio standards: penalties vary by province.
exceptions: Federal carbon pricing backstop applies where provincial system insufficient
Interprovincial electricity trade governed by federal jurisdiction
Offshore wind and tidal power remain emerging sectors

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Nunavut's electricity comes from renewable/non-emitting sources?
quiz.explanation: Approximately ~3% (renewable pilot projects) of Nunavut's electricity generation comes from renewable or non-emitting sources.

laws.title: Single-Use Plastics — Federal & Provincial Bans
laws.subtitle: Single-use Plastics Prohibition Regulations (SOR/2022-138) — Federal ban
laws.fullDescription: Canada's federal Single-use Plastics Prohibition Regulations (2022) banned checkout bags, cutlery, stir sticks, straws (with exceptions), six-pack rings, and food service containers made with problematic plastics. Nunavut: Nunavut adopted the federal single-use plastics ban. Waste management is extremely challenging in remote communities — everything must be shipped or burned.
laws.penalty: Federal violations: fines up to $1M (first offence). Provincial penalties additional.
exceptions: Medical straws still available
Reusable bags, cutlery, and containers permitted
Provinces may add additional restrictions

quiz.q: When did Canada's federal ban on many single-use plastics take effect?
quiz.explanation: Canada's federal Single-use Plastics Prohibition Regulations took effect in 2022, banning checkout bags, straws, cutlery, and more.

laws.title: Beverage Container Deposit System
laws.subtitle: Waste Reduction and Recovery Act (Nunavut) — Deposit-return program
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut operates a beverage container deposit-return program, though logistics in remote Arctic communities create unique challenges. Deposit-return systems incentivize recycling of beverage containers.
laws.penalty: Retailers accepting containers without paying deposit: fines.
exceptions: Program may be administered by industry or government
Deposits vary by container type and size
Not all container types included in all provinces

quiz.q: Does Nunavut have a beverage container deposit-return system?
options: Yes — small deposit on select containers
quiz.explanation: Nunavut has a beverage container deposit-return program, with logistical challenges given remote Arctic communities.

laws.title: Animal Cruelty — Criminal Code & Provincial Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code ss. 444–447 + Animal Protection Act (Nunavut) — Dual protection
laws.fullDescription: Animal cruelty is addressed by both federal Criminal Code (ss. 444–447) and provincial legislation. Nunavut: Nunavut's Animal Protection Act prohibits cruelty and neglect. Traditional Inuit harvesting of wildlife is recognized and protected under treaty rights. Criminal Code amendments in Bill C-84 (2019) strengthened anti-bestiality and animal fighting provisions.
laws.penalty: Up to $10,000 fine.
exceptions: Veterinary procedures and regulated farming practices exempt
Hunting and fishing with valid licences exempt
Scientific research with ethics approval exempt

quiz.q: How is animal cruelty law structured in Canada?
options: Both federal (Criminal Code) and provincial laws apply
quiz.explanation: Animal cruelty is governed by both federal Criminal Code provisions and provincial statutes, providing overlapping protections.

laws.title: Exotic & Dangerous Pets
laws.subtitle: Wildlife Act (Nunavut) — Regulated; Inuit harvesting rights recognized
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: Nunavut prohibits keeping most wildlife. Inuit rights to harvest polar bears, narwhals, caribou, and other species are protected under the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement. CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) governs importation federally.
laws.penalty: Keeping prohibited species: fines + seizure of animal.
exceptions: Licensed zoos and wildlife facilities exempt
Research institutions with permits exempt
CITES-listed species require federal import permits regardless of provincial rules

quiz.q: Are dangerous exotic animals (lions, tigers, large primates) generally legal as pets in Nunavut?
options: No or heavily restricted — dangerous exotic animals prohibited or tightly controlled
quiz.explanation: In Nunavut, dangerous exotic animals are generally prohibited or require special permits. Most provinces ban large predators and primates as pets.

laws.title: Fireworks — Consumer Regulations
laws.subtitle: Explosives Act (federal) + Fire Prevention Act (Nunavut) / Hamlet by-laws — Permits often required
laws.fullDescription: Consumer fireworks (F1 class) are legal across Canada for adults. Display fireworks require a federal permit. Nunavut: Consumer fireworks permitted; extreme fire risk in northern communities and limited firefighting capacity creates additional restrictions.
laws.penalty: Consumer fireworks violations: municipal fines. Display without permit: federal penalty.
exceptions: Professional display fireworks require permit and certified operator
Municipal bylaws may restrict use to specific dates/locations
F1 (lowest hazard) consumer fireworks widely available

quiz.q: What category of fireworks do Canadians need a federal permit to use?
quiz.explanation: Consumer fireworks (F1 class) can be used without a federal permit, but display fireworks require a permit under the federal Explosives Act.

laws.title: Gambling — Provincial Monopoly
laws.subtitle: Lotteries Act (Nunavut) — Provinces control gambling
laws.fullDescription: Under the Criminal Code (s. 207), provinces have exclusive authority to license and conduct gambling within their borders. Nunavut: Gaming and lottery regulated by territorial government; primarily through interprovincial lottery. Alcohol is restricted in many communities through plebiscites. Online gambling is permitted through provincially operated platforms (e.g., OLG, PlayNow, Loto-Québec).
laws.penalty: Illegal gambling operations: Criminal Code ss. 201–206, up to 2 years.
exceptions: Private/social gambling among friends (no rake) generally not criminal
Federally regulated horse racing
First Nations may operate gaming on reserve under provincial agreements

quiz.q: Under Canadian law, which level of government controls and licenses gambling?
quiz.explanation: Criminal Code s. 207 gives provinces exclusive authority to operate and license gambling within their borders.

laws.title: Net Neutrality — CRTC Regulation
laws.subtitle: Telecommunications Act + CRTC 2017-104 — Net neutrality upheld
laws.fullDescription: Net neutrality in Canada is enforced by the CRTC (Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission) under the Telecommunications Act. The CRTC's 2017 decision (2017-104) found differential pricing practices (zero-rating) that favour certain content to be unjust discrimination. Nunavut benefits from federal CRTC net neutrality protections. Internet access in Nunavut relies on satellite and is among the most expensive and slowest in Canada.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant ISPs: CRTC orders, fines under Telecom Act.
exceptions: CRTC may grant exemptions for technical traffic management practices
Internet service is regulated federally — provinces have no separate net neutrality laws
Differential pricing decisions reviewed case-by-case

quiz.q: Which body enforces net neutrality rules in Canada?
quiz.explanation: The CRTC regulates telecommunications in Canada and enforces net neutrality principles under the Telecommunications Act.

laws.title: Right to Repair — Emerging Legislation
laws.subtitle: Federal Bill C-244 (2023) — Limited — federal copyright exception
laws.fullDescription: Nunavut: No Nunavut-specific right-to-repair legislation. Canada is behind the EU and some US states on right-to-repair legislation. Federal Bill C-244 (2022) created a copyright exception for device diagnosis/repair but has not advanced.
laws.penalty: Varies — emerging area.
exceptions: Bill C-244 passed in 2023 — copyright exception for repair diagnostic tools
Agricultural equipment repairs may have specific provisions
Manufacturers still often restrict authorized repair networks

quiz.q: Did Canada pass any right-to-repair legislation at the federal level as of 2024?
options: Yes — comprehensive right to repair law
Yes — Bill C-244 created a copyright exception for device repair
Only Quebec has right to repair
quiz.explanation: Bill C-244 (2023) created a copyright exception allowing repair of devices for diagnostic/maintenance purposes — a limited but real step toward right to repair in Canada.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Rights — Human Rights & Beyond
laws.subtitle: Human Rights Act (Nunavut) + Canadian Human Rights Act — Comprehensive protections
laws.fullDescription: Canada has some of the world's strongest LGBTQ+ legal protections. The Canadian Human Rights Act and all provincial human rights codes prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2005 (Civil Marriage Act). Nunavut: Nunavut Human Rights Act protects sexual orientation and gender identity. Two-spirit identities are recognized within Inuit cultural traditions. Conversion therapy banned federally 2022.
laws.penalty: Discrimination: human rights complaints, damages, reinstatement. Conversion therapy (federally banned 2022): up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Conversion therapy banned federally (Bill C-4, 2022)
Transgender persons can change legal gender federally without surgery (Bill C-16, 2017)
Religious/educational institutions may claim limited exemptions in some provinces

quiz.q: When did same-sex marriage become legal across all of Canada?
quiz.explanation: Canada legalized same-sex marriage nationwide through the Civil Marriage Act in 2005, making it one of the first countries to do so.
